[Objection:] If the relation meant is one characterized by conjunction [of word and meaning] — [then we say:] relations such as cause-and-effect, ground-and-consequence, substrate-and-superstratum, maternal kinship, and the like are simply untenable for words.
[Reply:] It is said: The one relation that is being designated here you, sir, do not designate — namely, the relation between the signified and the signifier, which has the character of name and named. [Objector] says: If the word is a signifier, why does it not signify when heard for the first time? [Reply:] Our observation is the authority everywhere. For we understand [something to be] a 'signifier' by seeing [its] signification — not [by the fact that] 'it was heard for the first time,' since at the first hearing, signification is not seen. The comprehension of meaning comes from hearing [the word] however many times [it takes]. Just as the eye, being a seer, does not illuminate without external light — but it does not thereby become a non-seer.
If [the word] heard for the first time does not signify, then the relation of word with meaning is constructed [i.e., conventional]. Why? Because these two — word and meaning — are by nature unrelated. For we perceive the word in the mouth and the meaning on the ground. And they designate: 'This is a word, not an object; this is an object, not a word.' There is also a difference in form: they pronounce this word 'cow' (<s>go</s>) [but] understand an object possessing a dewlap and so forth. And the relation between two things that are separate is observed to be constructed, like that between a rope and a pot. Now, what is the word in 'cow' (<s>gaur</s>)? The venerable <s>Upavarṣa</s> [says]: the syllables <s>g</s>, <s>au</s>, and <s>visarjanīya</s>. For the term 'word' (<s>śabda</s>) is well-known in the world for that which is apprehended by the ear. And those [syllables] are apprehended by the ear.
If so, the cognition of meaning is not established. How? For the meaning is not apprehended from the cognition of each syllable individually. Nor is there any aggregate distinct from the syllables from which the cognition of meaning could arise. For when the <s>g</s>-sound [is present], the <s>au</s>-sound and <s>visarjanīya</s> are not [present]; when the <s>au</s>-sound and <s>visarjanīya</s> [are present], the <s>g</s>-sound is not. Therefore, there is no other word 'cow' distinct from the syllables <s>g</s> etc., from which the cognition of meaning could arise. [Objection:] Even when the word has disappeared, there is cognition of meaning from memory. [Reply:] No. Since memory too is momentary, it has the same [defect] as the syllables.
[Reply:] The last syllable, accompanied by the impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) generated by the preceding syllables, is the signifier — thus there is no fault. [Objection:] But even so, the common expression 'we understand the meaning from the word' would be untenable.
[Reply:] It is said: If it is untenable, let it be untenable. For one cannot accept an object unestablished by perception and other [means of knowledge] merely because a common expression would [otherwise] be untenable. Common expressions are seen both with tenable meanings and untenable meanings — such as 'Devadatta, drive the cow' [tenable] and 'ten pomegranates, six cakes' [when there are not that many — untenable].
[Objection:] But the śāstra-authors too say thus: 'The verb (<s>ākhyāta</s>) expresses a state that is sequentially constituted' — as in 'he goes,' 'he cooks,' from inception to completion. [Reply:] Even the statement of a śāstra-author is not sufficient to establish this unsubstantiated meaning.
Moreover, this [expression 'from the word'] is not really untenable. The impressions arise from the syllables; from the impressions arises the cognition of meaning — thus the syllables are indeed the cause of the cognition of meaning. [Objection:] If this is said to be a secondary usage (<s>gauṇa</s>) — [Reply:] No, the causal role of the syllables is not secondary, because [the cognition of meaning] exists when they exist and does not exist when they do not exist. And even if it were secondary, one cannot fabricate an object unestablished by perception and the like merely [to avoid] a secondary usage. For when one says 'fire is the boy,' one does not conclude that the word 'fire' should not be secondary, and therefore combustion itself is the boy. Nor is any other word 'cow' directly perceived as distinct from the syllables <s>g</s> etc., because no difference is perceived and because identity is perceived. For the syllables <s>g</s> etc. are directly perceived. Therefore, 'cow' (<s>gaur</s>) is the word consisting of syllables ending in <s>visarjanīya</s> — the syllables themselves. There is no other entity called 'word' distinct from them. [Objection:] But in postulating impressions too there is a postulation of something unseen. [Reply:] In postulating [a separate] word, there would be both that [unseen postulation] and the postulation of a word. Therefore, the syllables alone constitute the word.
Now, what is the meaning of this word 'cow'? We say: the universal form (<s>ākṛti</s>) qualified by dewlap and the like. [Objection:] But is the <s>ākṛti</s> established or not? [Reply:] Being directly perceived, it does not need to be established. For one directly sees [patterns like] 'bracelet,' 'svastika,' 'vardhamānaka.' [Objection:] This is delusion. [Reply:] No. One cannot say there is delusion when there is no reversal of the cognition.
[Buddhist objection:] Even in the absence of a [real] separate entity, there arises a cognition of this kind — 'row,' 'flock,' 'forest' — [showing that a universal can be cognized without a real referent]. [Reply:] No. This statement is irrelevant. Is the claim that, in the absence of the forest, a forest-cognition arises — i.e., is even perception being challenged, [implying] that even trees do not exist? If so, then this is the <s>Mahāyānika</s> (Mahāyāna Buddhist) position, which has already been refuted. Or is it that the proponent of the reality of <s>ākṛtis</s> is being criticized — [meaning] 'your other thesis is flawed'? [We reply:] Even if the forest does not [separately] exist for you, the forest-cognition still applies [to you]. Moreover, being unable to refute the thesis at hand, your pointing out a flaw in a different thesis constitutes a point of defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>), because it fails to prove [anything]. For he [the opponent] will say: 'Let it be flawed, if it is flawed. How does that flaw or non-flaw prove your thesis or refute mine?' And since no forest is apprehended apart from the trees, we understand from that very [fact] that [a separate entity called] 'forest' does not exist. If, in the case of a forest, a cognition contrary to its real existence arises from some other reason, then from that [contrary cognition] we understand 'this forest-cognition is false; therefore the forest does not exist.' But the cognition regarding cows and the like is never reversed. Hence the disparity. Or alternatively, if even in the case of forests and the like there is no reversal of cognition, then they too exist. Therefore, the mention of rows and forests is irrelevant.
Thus <s>Jaimini</s>'s statement is established: <s>ākṛti</s> (universal form) is the meaning of words. And how <s>ākṛti</s> is the meaning of words, we shall establish more thoroughly later on.
Now, what is the relation? It is that by which, when the word is known, the meaning is known.
But that [relation] is constructed — this was argued above. Therefore, we believe that some person, having established a relation between words and meanings, composed the <s>Vedas</s> for the purpose of communication.
To this it is now said: Because the relation is not man-made (<s>apauruṣeya</s>), [the thesis] is established. But how is this known — that this relation is not man-made? Because there is no author of the relation. How is there no author? Because there is no evidence from perception, which is a valid means of knowledge, and because the other [means of knowledge] are based on perception.
[Objection:] Perhaps, because of its great antiquity, [the authorship] might be beyond the perceptual range of present-day people. [Reply:] That which is of great antiquity would not fail to be remembered. For the <s>Himālayas</s> and the like are not forgotten as wells and gardens are. For in those [wells and gardens], the separation of people [from them] occurs through the destruction of a place or the destruction of a lineage. But there is no separation of people from the practice of word-meaning communication. [Objection:] Perhaps people, being concerned only with the practice of the relation, would forget the author, disregarding the purposeless remembrance of the author. [Reply:] No. For if a person, having created the relation, were to communicate [through it], the creator would necessarily be remembered at the time of communication. For the purpose [of communication] is accomplished when both creator and user agree, not when they disagree. For by the word <s>vṛddhi</s>, one who does not follow <s>Pāṇini</s>'s usage would not understand '<s>ādaic</s>' [the augmented vowels]; nor would one who does not accept <s>Pāṇini</s>'s system [understand it]. Similarly, even by the syllable <s>m</s>, one who does not follow <s>Piṅgala</s>'s usage would not understand 'a triad consisting entirely of heavy syllables'; nor would one who does not accept <s>Piṅgala</s>'s system. Therefore, both creator and user must agree. Therefore, those who communicate using the <s>Vedas</s> would necessarily remember the creator of the relation and of the communication. For when the creator of the <s>sūtra</s> '<s>vṛddhir ādaic</s>' is forgotten, nothing at all would be understood from it — [namely the meaning] 'that word whose initial is one of these [augmented vowels] is called <s>vṛddha</s>.' Therefore, from the absence of such remembrance, we conclude: no one composed the <s>Vedas</s> having first created a relation between words and meanings for the purpose of communication.
And even if forgetting were possible, still, without a means of valid knowledge, we would not accept an author of the relation — just as, even though the non-perception of an existing thing does occur, we would not on that account alone, without a means of valid knowledge, accept a hare's horn. Therefore, the relation of word with meaning is not man-made (<s>apauruṣeya</s>).
[Objection:] We would establish an author of the relation through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption). For we do not observe anyone understanding meaning from a word whose relation [with meaning] has not been established. And if they could, they would understand even at the first hearing. From the non-perception of that [understanding at first hearing], we conclude that there must be an author of the relation.
[Reply:] No. It is already accomplished through instruction (<s>upadeśa</s>). If, in the absence of an author [of the relation], meanings were necessarily not apprehended, then we would know the author through <s>arthāpatti</s>. But there is another way: children, overhearing elders communicating in their own affairs and directly perceiving the objects [referred to], are seen to learn [the meanings]. Those elders too, when they were children, [learned] from other elders; those too from others — and thus there is no beginning. Or alternatively, it may be that not even a single word was ever [first] associated with a meaning, and then some [person] initiated the associations. [Reply to this:] When the practice of elders exists, the authorship of the relation is not necessitated by the facts. Moreover, those who advocate the practice of elders point to direct experience, while the others fabricate an author. And fabrication is not sound when there is a counter-instance in direct experience. Therefore, there is no author [of the relation]. And [the word-meaning relation is] without deviation.
Just as in this country the word 'cow' (<s>go</s>) applies to [an animal] possessing a dewlap and the like, so too in all [regions], even inaccessible ones. How could multiple authors agree [on the same conventions]? Even a single one could not [accomplish this]. Therefore, there is no author.
Another [authority] says: 'And [the relation is] without deviation.'
For there is no time devoid of the relation when no word was associated with any meaning. How? For the very act of creating the relation is untenable. The one creating the relation would necessarily have to use some word [to do so]. And by what [word] would the relation of that [word itself] have been created? If by some other [word], then by what [was the relation of] that [other word created]? — and so on, without end. Therefore, the one creating the relation must necessarily accept that some words, whose relation [with meaning] is established through the practice of elders, exist without having been created [by anyone]. If such establishment through practice exists, then there is no necessity for an author — and thus even the argument from <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) fails. [Objection:] How would children whose relations [between words and meanings] are not [yet] established learn from elders? [Reply:] What is directly observed cannot be called untenable. For children are directly observed learning from elders — but no one has observed them [learning from] an uncomprehended author of the relation. Hence the disparity.
'Regarding an object that is not apprehended' — And when the object — deities and the like — is not apprehended, the creation of names is both purposeless and impossible. For names are created for the purpose of communicating distinctions and with reference to those distinctions. Therefore, when the distinctions are unknown, both [creating names and communicating] are impossible. Therefore, the relation of word with meaning is not man-made (<s>apauruṣeya</s>).
And therefore: 'That is a valid means of knowledge, because of its independence.' For when this is so, [the Veda] does not depend on another person or another cognition. Therefore, <s>Dharma</s> is characterized by Vedic injunction alone and by no other characteristic.
The mention of <s>Bādarāyaṇa</s> has been explained.
Now, as to what was said — 'Word is not a means [of knowing <s>Dharma</s>], because the result is not seen at the time of the ritual action, and because the action does not exist at a later time' — to that it is said: It would not be a means of knowledge if there were only five means of knowledge. But whatever it is by which something is ascertained — that is a means of knowledge. And by words too things are ascertained; therefore, word too is a means of knowledge, just as perception is. Nor does the fact that something established by one means of knowledge is not established by another mean that it is not established [at all]. Nor is it thus stated [in the Veda] that 'when the action has been performed, the result occurs at that very time'; rather, [the statement is that] 'by the action the result is obtained.' And as for [the objection] that at a later time there is another perceptible cause of the result — that is no fault. For that [other cause] and the [Vedic] word are both causes there.
As for the statement adduced as contradicting perception — 'This sacrificer, armed with sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world' — [where it is said] perception indicates the body [and hence the body cannot go to heaven]:
To that it is said: Because of the connection with the body — he whose body it is, he too, being 'armed with sacrificial implements,' is designated [as going to heaven].
[Objector] says: Who is this other [entity]? We do not perceive him.
[Reply:] But we perceive him through the vital breaths and the like. He who breathes in, breathes out, exhales, blinks, and so forth — he, being in this body, is 'armed with sacrificial implements.' [Objection:] But it is the body itself that breathes in and out! [Reply:] No, the vital breaths and the like are not properties of the body. For they are contrary in nature to the properties of the body, since they do not last as long as the body. The properties of the body — form and the like — last as long as the body. But the vital breaths do not exist even when the body exists. Therefore, the vital breaths are not properties of the body. Moreover, pleasure and the like are perceived by oneself, not by another as properties of the body [are perceived], like form and the like. Therefore, because of the dissimilarity with the properties of the body, [the sacrificer] is other than the body — he is 'armed with sacrificial implements.'
[Buddhist] says: Whence comes this conviction that there exists, distinct from pleasure and the like, something that possesses them? For we do not perceive its intrinsic nature by setting aside pleasure and the like. Therefore, it does not exist, like a hare's horn.
Then it is said: Without him, whose would pleasure and the like be?
[Buddhist replies:] We shall say: 'Nobody's.' For it is not the case that whatever is perceived must necessarily have a possessor. For one whose relation is also perceived and whose possessor [is also perceived] — in that case, 'this is its possessor' is understood. But upon perceiving the moon or the sun, there is no search for another possessor — 'whose is this?' It is determined to be nobody's. Therefore, there is nothing distinct from pleasure and the like that possesses them. And if a possessor must necessarily be postulated for whatever is perceived, then, having perceived the self itself in this manner, we would search for yet another possessor — 'whose is this?' And having postulated that one, we would postulate another, and another — resulting in an infinite regress. But if, having postulated one, you will not postulate yet another possessor, and will stop at just that much and be satisfied with just that much — then be satisfied at the level of consciousness itself and stop at just that much.
To this it is said: If there is no knower other than cognition, then who is it that 'knows'? The designation of an agent of knowledge is established by this word [the verb 'knows']. Therefore, this word is meaningful, and [to explain it] we shall postulate a self distinct from cognition.
[Buddhist] says: The gods will make this word meaningful, if they think it needs to be made meaningful! For many people here, being proponents of the existence of the self, saying 'the self exists, the self exists,' are direct speakers of the word [claiming self-existence] — yet even so, they do not succeed in establishing the existence of the self. How much less, then, from the observation of the indirect word 'knows'! Therefore, this [argument] is unfounded.
[Reply:] It is said: We perceive the self through desire (<s>icchā</s>). How? For desire arises with regard to something previously perceived, not something not previously perceived. Just as we have no desire for those sweet tree-fruits beyond Mount <s>Meru</s> to the north that have never been perceived by people of our kind. Nor does one person have desire for an object perceived by another person but not perceived by oneself. But desire does arise the next day for what was perceived the day before. Therefore, we understand that [desire] has the same agent as that [prior] perception. If mere cognition were the perceiver, then when it has perished, whose desire would arise the next day? But if the knower is eternal and distinct from cognition, then the same one who perceived on one day will desire on the next. Otherwise, desire would be untenable.
To this [the Buddhist] says: Where is our conviction that [something] is 'untenable'? [Only] in what is not established by a means of valid knowledge. We do not, to begin with, perceive anything other than cognition. And what we do not perceive, we understand to be non-existent, like a hare's horn. Nor is the existence of cognition untenable in its absence [i.e., the absence of a self], precisely because [cognition] is established by direct experience. And its momentariness too is based on direct experience alone. Nor, when there is no knower other than cognition and cognition is impermanent, is desire the next day untenable — precisely because it is established by direct experience. Moreover, this has not been observed — that the very same one who perceived the day before desires the next day. But this has been observed: in some cases, one person sees and another desires; in other cases, not. Within the same continuum (<s>santati</s>), one [moment] desires; in a different continuum, [it] does not. Therefore, there is nothing distinct from pleasure and the like.
To this it is said: It is not tenable that non-rememberers would desire. Nor does memory arise regarding something never previously seen. Therefore, in [the theory of] a merely momentary aggregate of cognitions (<s>vijñānaskandha</s>), memory is untenable.
To this [the Buddhist] says: Memory too is like desire. A cognition similar to a prior cognition, or [having] the object of a prior cognition — that is called memory. And that [memory], even when the seer has perished, arising the next day, is not untenable — precisely because it is established by direct experience. The cognition that arises in one aggregate of [momentary] factors from another aggregate is perceived by [a factor] born of the same continuum, not by one of a different continuum. Therefore, the aggregates are empty [of a self]. And on this point there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> passage: 'It is a mass of cognition (<s>vijñānaghana</s>) that arises from these elements and perishes along with them; after death there is no consciousness.'
To this it is said: This is not so. Regarding what was seen the day before, the cognition arises the next day: 'I saw this.' And this occurs with respect to the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>), not with respect to another. For that other is one who saw the day before [i.e., a perished moment]. Therefore, there exists something other than that [perished cognition], to which this word 'I' applies.
[Buddhist] says: The word 'I' is seen applied to other [things] too, by secondary usage — as in 'I am the son,' 'I am <s>Devadatta</s>,' 'I am going.'
To this it is said: We do not cite as evidence the word 'I' as applied to other objects, but rather the re-cognition (<s>pratybhijñā</s>) that is distinct from the word. For we recognize: 'We ourselves perceived this object the day before; we ourselves remember it today.' Therefore: 'We ourselves understand this object; we are the same as yesterday, we are the same as today.' And those who are the same yesterday and today have not perished. Moreover, on this point there are <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> passages: 'This indeed is the self' — they traditionally teach it as having the nature of indestructibility: 'it is not worn out, for it does not wear out.' And also: 'This self is indeed imperishable, having the nature of non-annihilation.' But cognition is perishable. Therefore, we understand that [the self] is other than the perishable [cognition]. Nor can one maintain: 'Objects are not as they are perceived, and are as they are not perceived' — for then it would follow that 'the hare does not exist, [but] the hare's horn does exist.' And the I-cognition cannot be called delusion, because there is no sublating cognition. Therefore, [the self] exists as distinct from pleasure and the like. And if so, he is the one designated as 'armed with sacrificial implements.'
[Buddhist] says: If there exists a knower other than cognition, let it be shown apart from cognition — 'This is it, of such-and-such nature.' But it cannot be shown. Therefore, nothing other than [cognition] exists.
To this it is said: He is self-illuminating (<s>svasaṃvedya</s>). He cannot be seen by another. How could he be shown? Just as a sighted person himself sees a form but cannot show it to another who is congenitally blind — and the fact that it cannot be shown does not lead to the conclusion that it does not exist — so too this person himself perceives the self but cannot show it to another, because the other perceiver lacks the capacity to see that person [directly]. That other person too perceives his own self, not the self of another. Therefore, all [persons], perceiving the self each through their own self, exist — even though they are not perceived by other persons. And on this point there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> passage: 'When speech has subsided, what light does this person have? He has the self as his light, O King' — thus he said. And that he is not perceived by another — on this point too there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> passage: 'Ungraspable, for he is not grasped.' The purport is: he is not grasped by another. Why? Because of the statement that he is self-luminous. And on this point too there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> passage: 'Here this person is self-luminous.'
By what means, then, is he communicated to another? On this method too there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> passage: 'This is the self — [described as] \"not this, not this" — thus he said.' He cannot be shown as 'he is of such form.' But what another perceives — the negation of that is the method of teaching him. The other perceives the body. Therefore the self is taught [by negation]: 'The body is not the self; there is something other than the body — and that is the self' — thus, through the negation of the body, the self is taught. Similarly, the vital breaths and the like are not the self — through their negation, something other than them is taught. Likewise, pleasure and the like, which belong to another [i.e., are perceived by others through signs] — they too are not the self; through their negation, something other than them is taught.
That the one who sees [is the self] himself and not some other person — this too is inferred from purposeful activity: when that person strives to settle matters left unfinished the day before and to complete remaining tasks, from this activity we understand: 'Surely this [person] perceives impermanent things as permanent [i.e., persistent].'
It is also taught through analogy (<s>upamāna</s>): 'The kind of thing you yourself perceive your self to be — understand by this analogy that I too perceive exactly the same kind of thing' — just as someone would describe his own sensation to another: 'I feel as if I am burning; I feel as if I am being carried; I feel as if I am being obstructed.' Therefore, because [the self] is perceived by oneself, there exists a person (<s>puruṣa</s>) distinct from that [cognition, pleasure, etc.].
As for what was said — 'Let it be shown apart from cognition' — if you are precluding the very means, it is impossible to reach the goal without the means. The means for knowing things is precisely this: each thing is known in the manner in which it is known — and that is how it is. For example: What is white? That in which whiteness exists. What is whiteness? That which is the basis for the application of the word 'white.' Where is its application? That which is understood when the word 'white' is uttered. Therefore, one cannot show the nature of anything by setting aside cognition.
Nor does it follow that when a cognition is necessarily apprehended, the object of cognition is [thereby] necessarily apprehended. For even when the cognition is not apprehended, the object can be apprehended. For it is not the case that cognition is directly perceived [as an object] — rather, the knowable object is directly perceived. This was stated earlier. Therefore, if [one wants to] deny what must be denied, let him deny cognition [rather than] the object — this too was already stated. Therefore, there exists a person (<s>puruṣa</s>) who is eternal and distinct from pleasure and the like.
As for the statement 'It is a mass of cognition that arises from these elements and perishes along with them; after death there is no consciousness' — to this it is said: In this very [passage], [<s>Yājñavalkya</s>] addressed [<s>Maitreyī</s> who] said 'You have bewildered me, lord!' — and in the response after this challenge, having disclaimed the purport of bewilderment, he explained: 'I do not speak bewilderment; indeed this self is imperishable, having the nature of non-annihilation — but it has contact with sense-faculties.' Therefore, [the self] is not mere cognition. Hence the disparity.
As for what was said — 'This one does not go [to heaven]' — [objecting that this] is an injunctive word: let it not be an injunctive word. What is established by another statement — 'Let the one desiring heaven sacrifice' — is [merely] being restated. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

children.translated_text: [CRITICAL APPARATUS: Textual variants and manuscript readings for the commentary on Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.4-1.1.5, collating editions E1-E6, manuscripts TA, TB, TC, A, and secondary sources (TSP, Kāśikā, Nyāya-ratnākara, Tātparya-ṭīkā). Notes cover variant readings for key philosophical terms including utpatti, saṃbandha, pratyakṣa, and discussions of Bādarāyaṇa's positions on perception and valid cognition.]

children.text: karmaike tatra darśanāt // MS_1,1.6 //
children.translated_text: Some [hold that sound is] a product, because it is observed [to arise only after effort]. // MS 1.1.6 //

children.text:
uktam - nityaḥ śabdārthayoḥ saṃbandha iti. tad anupapannam, śabdasyānityatvāt. vinaṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ, punar asya kriyamāṇasyārthenākṛtakaḥ saṃbandho nopapadyate. na hi prathamaśrutāc chabdāt kaścid arthaṃ pratyeti. kathaṃ punar anityaḥ śabdaḥ. prayatnād uttarakālaṃ dṛśyate yataḥ. ataḥ prayatnānantaryāt tena kriyata iti gamyate.
nanv abhivyañjyāt sa enam. neti brūmaḥ. na hy asya prāg abhivyañjanāt sadbhāve kiṃcana pramāṇam asti. saṃś cābhivyajyate nāsan.
children.translated_text:
It was stated that the relation between word and meaning is innate. That is untenable, because sound (<s>śabda</s>) is non-eternal. [Since] sound perishes, when it is produced again, an uncreated relation with meaning is impossible. For no one understands a meaning from a sound heard for the first time. But how is sound non-eternal? Because it is observed only after effort. Therefore, since it appears only after effort, we infer that it is produced by that [effort].
[Objection:] But perhaps [effort merely] manifests it. [Reply:] We say no. For there is no evidence whatsoever of its existence prior to manifestation. And something non-existent is not manifested.

children.text: asthānāt // MS_1,1.7 //
children.translated_text: Because [it is perceived] from no [fixed] location. // MS 1.1.7 //

children.text: no{*1/322*} khalv apy uccaritaṃ muhūrtam apy upalabhāmahe. ato vinaṣṭa ity avagacchāmaḥ. na ca san nopalabhyate. anupalaṃbhakāraṇānāṃ vyavadhānādīnām abhāve 'py anupalambhanāt. na cāsau viṣayam aprāptaḥ, ākāśāviṣayatvāt, karṇacchidre 'py anupalambhanāt.
children.translated_text: Moreover, we do not perceive [sound] even for a moment after it has been uttered. Therefore, we understand that it has perished. And what exists is not [in a case where it is] not perceived. Because it is not perceived even in the absence of obstructing causes such as intervening barriers. Nor is it [the case] that [sound] has not reached its object — because sound has space (<s>ākāśa</s>) as its locus, and even in the opening of the ear, it is not perceived [after utterance].

children.text:
NOTES:
*{1/322: E1 gibt als v.l.: na cainam uccaritaṃ}*
children.translated_text: NOTES: [Textual variant: E1 gives as variant reading: 'nor that one, once uttered']

children.text: karotiśabdāt // MS_1,1.8 //
children.translated_text: Because of the use of the word 'to make' (<s>karoti</s>). // MS 1.1.8 //

children.text: api ca śabdaṃ kuru, mā śabdaṃ kārṣīr iti vyavahartāraḥ prayuñjate, na te nūnam avagacchanti sa evāyaṃ śabda iti.
children.translated_text: Moreover, people in ordinary usage employ [expressions such as] 'make a sound' and 'do not make a sound' — they surely do not understand [the sound to be] 'this very same sound [as before].'

children.text: sattvāntare ca yaugapadyāt // MS_1,1.9 //
children.translated_text: And because of simultaneity in different beings. // MS 1.1.9 //

children.text: nānādeśeṣu ca yugapac chabdam upalabhāmahe, tad ekasya nityasyānupapannam iti. asati viśeṣe nityasya nānekatvam. kāryāṇāṃ tu bahūnāṃ nānādeśeṣu kriyamāṇānām upapadyate 'nekadeśasaṃbandhaḥ. tasmād apy anityaḥ.
children.translated_text: And we perceive sound simultaneously in various places. That is impossible for a single eternal [entity]. In the absence of a differentiating factor, an eternal [entity] cannot be many. But for products — many [sounds] being produced in different places — the connection with multiple locations is possible. Therefore, from this too, [sound is] non-eternal.

children.text: prakṛtivikṛtyoś ca // MS_1,1.10 //
children.translated_text: And because of the [relation of] original form and modification (<s>prakṛti</s> and <s>vikṛti</s>). // MS 1.1.10 //

children.text: api ca dadhyatrety atrekāraḥ prakṛtiḥ, yakāro vikṛtir ity upapadiśanti. yad vikriyate, tad anityam. ikārasādṛśyaṃ ca yakārasyopalabhyate, tenāpi tayoḥ prakṛtivikārabhāvo lakṣyate.
children.translated_text: Moreover, in the word '<s>dadhyatra</s>' (ghee here), they teach that the '<s>i</s>'-sound is the original form (<s>prakṛti</s>) and the '<s>y</s>'-sound is the modification (<s>vikṛti</s>). What is modified is non-eternal. And a similarity between the '<s>i</s>'-sound and the '<s>y</s>'-sound is perceived, whereby their relation as original and modified is recognized.

children.text: vṛddhiś ca kartṛbhūmnāsya // MS_1,1.11 //
children.translated_text: And [because of] the increase [of sound] through the multiplicity of producers. // MS 1.1.11 //

children.text: api ca bahubhir uccārayadbhir mahān śabdaḥ śrūyate. sa yady abhivyajyate, bahubhir alpaiś coccāryamāṇas tāvān evopalabhyeta. ato manyāmahe nūnam asyaikaikena kaścid avayavaḥ kriyate, yat pracayād ayaṃ mahān upalabhyate.
children.translated_text: Moreover, when many persons utter [a sound], a loud sound is heard. If [sound is merely] manifested, then whether uttered by many or by few, it should be perceived as exactly the same. Therefore, we think that each individual produces some component [of the sound], and from their accumulation, this [sound] is perceived as loud.
Page 26
NOTES: [Edition cross-references: E2: 1,90; E5: 1,272; E6: 1,19]

children.text: samaṃ tu tatra darśanam // MS_1,1.12 //
children.translated_text: But the observation [of arising after effort] is the same in both cases. // MS 1.1.12 //

children.text: tuśabdāt pakṣo viparivartate. yad{*1/324*} uktam - prayatnād uttarakāle darśanāt kṛtako 'yam iti{*1/325*}. yadi vispaṣṭena hetunā śabdasya nityatvaṃ vaktuṃ śakṣyāmaḥ, tato nityapratyayasāmarthyāt prayatnenābhivyajyata iti bhaviṣyati. yadi prāg uccāraṇād anabhivyaktaḥ prayatnenābhivyajyate. tasmād ubhayoḥ pakṣayoḥ samam etat.
children.translated_text: The word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) reverses the position. What was said — 'Because it is observed after effort, this [sound] is a product.' If we can state the eternality of sound with a clear reason, then, by the force of the conviction of eternality, [the conclusion] 'it is manifested by effort' will follow. If, prior to utterance, it exists unmanifested and is manifested by effort — then this observation [of arising after effort] is the same on both positions.
NOTES: [Textual variants for this passage across editions]

children.text: sataḥ param adarśanaṃ viṣayānāgamāt // MS_1,1.13 //
children.translated_text: The non-perception of what exists [is due to] the non-arrival of the sense-object. // MS 1.1.13 //

children.text:
yad aparaṃ kāraṇam uktam - uccaritapradhvasta iti{*1/326*}. atrāpi yadi śakṣyāmo nityatām asya vispaṣṭaṃ vaktum, tato nityapratyayasāmarthyāt kadācid upalambhaṃ kadācid anupalambhaṃ dṛṣṭvā kiṃcid upalambhasya nimittaṃ kalpayiṣyāmaḥ. tac ca saṃyogavibhāgasadbhāve sati bhavatīti saṃyogavibhāgāv evābhivyañjakāv iti vakṣyāmaḥ. uparatayoḥ saṃyogavibhāgayoḥ śrūyata iti cet. naitad evam. na nūnam uparamanti saṃyogavibhāgāḥ, yata upalabhyate śabda iti. na hi te pratyakṣā iti.
yadi śabdaṃ saṃyogavibhāgā evābhivyañjanti na kurvanti, ākāśaviṣayatvāc chabdasyākāśasyaikatvād ya evāyam atra śrotrākāśaḥ, sa eva deśāntareṣv apīti śrughnasthaiḥ{*1/327*} saṃyogavibhāgair abhivyaktaḥ pāṭaliputre 'py upalabhyeta.
yasya punaḥ kurvanti, tasya vāyavīyāḥ saṃyogavibhāgā vāyvāśritatvād vāyuṣv eva kariṣyanti, yathā tantavas tantuṣv eva paṭam. tasya pāṭaliputreṣv anupalambho yuktaḥ, śrughnasthatvāt teṣām. yasyāpy abhivyañjanti, tasyāpy eṣa na doṣaḥ, dūre satyāḥ karṇaśaṣkulyā anupakārakāḥ saṃyogavibhāgāḥ, tena dūre yac chrotraṃ tena nopalabhyata iti. naitad evam. aprāptāś cet [28]{*1/328*}saṃyogavibhāgāḥ śrotrasyopakuryuḥ. saṃnikṛṣṭavikṛṣṭadeśasthau yugapac chabdam upalabheyātām. na ca yugapad upalabhete. tasmān nāprāptā upakurvanti. na ced upakurvanti{*1/329*}, tasmād animittaṃ śabdopalambhane saṃyogavibhāgāv iti.
naitad evam. abhighātena hi preritā vāyavas timitāni{*1/330*} vāyvantarāṇi pratibādhamānāḥ sarvatodikkān saṃyogavibhāgān utpādayanti. yāvad vegam abhipratiṣṭhante. te ca vāyor apratyakṣatvāt saṃyogavibhāgā nopalabhyante. anuparateṣv eva teṣu śabda upalabhyate noparateṣu. ato na doṣaḥ. ata eva cānuvātaṃ dūrād upalabhyate śabdaḥ.
children.translated_text:
The other reason that was stated — 'it perishes after being uttered.' Here too, if we can clearly state its eternality, then, by the force of the conviction of eternality, observing sometimes perception and sometimes non-perception, we shall posit some cause for the perception. And that [cause] operates when conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) and disjunction (<s>vibhāga</s>) exist; therefore, we shall say that conjunction and disjunction alone are the manifesting agents. [Objection:] But when conjunction and disjunction have ceased, [the sound] is [still] heard! [Reply:] This is not so. Surely conjunctions and disjunctions do not cease [instantly], since the sound is [still] perceived. For they are not directly perceptible.
If conjunctions and disjunctions merely manifest sound and do not produce it — then, since sound has space (<s>ākāśa</s>) as its locus and space is one, the very same ear-space here would be the same in other places too — and so [a sound] manifested by conjunctions and disjunctions in <s>Śrughna</s> should be perceived in <s>Pāṭaliputra</s> as well.
But for one who [holds that conjunctions and disjunctions] produce [sound] — the aerial conjunctions and disjunctions, being dependent on wind, would produce [sound] in the winds themselves, just as threads [produce] a cloth in the threads themselves. For him, the non-perception in <s>Pāṭaliputra</s> is justified, since they are located in <s>Śrughna</s>.
For one who holds that they manifest [rather than produce], this is no defect either: when the ear-cavity is far away, the conjunctions and disjunctions are unable to assist [perception]; therefore, the [distant] ear does not perceive [the sound]. [Objection:] This is not so. If conjunctions and disjunctions that have not reached the ear could assist it, then persons located in nearby and distant places would perceive the sound simultaneously. But they do not perceive simultaneously. Therefore, those that have not reached [the ear] do not assist. And if they do not assist, then conjunction and disjunction are not the cause of the perception of sound.
[Reply:] This is not so. For the winds, set in motion by impact, striking against other winds that are still, generate conjunctions and disjunctions in all directions, as far as their momentum carries them. And those conjunctions and disjunctions, being of imperceptible wind, are not perceived. Only when those [conjunctions and disjunctions] have not yet ceased is sound perceived — not when they have ceased. Therefore, there is no defect. And for this very reason, sound is perceived from a greater distance when it travels downwind.

children.text: prayogasya param // MS_1,1.14 //
children.translated_text: The [word 'make'] refers to the application [of effort, not the production of sound itself]. // MS 1.1.14 //

children.text: yad aparaṃ kāraṇam uktam - śabdaṃ kuru mā kārṣīr iti vyavahartāraḥ prayuñjate{*1/331*}. yady asaṃśayaṃ nityaḥ śabdaḥ, śabdaprayogaṃ kurv iti bhaviṣyati, yathā gomayāt{*1/332*} kurv iti saṃhāre{*1/333*}.
children.translated_text: The other reason that was stated — 'People employ [the expression] "make a sound, do not make a sound."' If sound is undoubtedly eternal, then [the expression] 'make the application of sound' will be [the proper interpretation] — just as [one says] 'make [fire] from cow-dung,' meaning [applying it] in kindling.

children.text: ādityavad yaugapadyam // MS_1,1.15 //
children.translated_text: Simultaneity [in many places is] like the sun. // MS 1.1.15 //

children.text:
yat tv ekadeśasya{*1/334*} sato nānādeśeṣu yugapad darśanam anupapannam iti{*1/335*}. ādityaṃ paśya devānāṃpriya. ekaḥ sann anekadeśāv asthita iva lakṣyate. kathaṃ punar avagamyata eka āditya iti. ucyate - prāṅmukho devadattaḥ pūrvāhne saṃprati purastād ādityaṃ paśyati. tasya dakṣiṇato 'vasthito na dvau paśyati, ātmanaś ca saṃprati na tiraścīnaṃ{*1/336*} devadattasyārjave. [28]{*1/337*} tasmād eka āditya iti. dūratvād asya deśo nāvadhāryate. ato vyāmohaḥ. evaṃ śabde 'pi vyāmohād anavadhāraṇaṃ deśasya. yadi śrotraṃ saṃyogavibhāgadeśam āgatya śabdaṃ gṛhṇīyāt, tathāpi tāvad anekadeśatā kadācid avagamyeta. na ca tatsaṃyogadeśam āgacchati. pratyakṣā hi karṇaśaṣkulī taddeśā
gṛhyate. vāyavīyāḥ punaḥ saṃyogavibhāgā apratyakṣasya vāyoḥ, karṇaśaṣkulīpradeśe prādurbhavanto nopalabhyanta iti nānupapannam. ata eva vyāmoho yan nānādeśeṣu śabda iti. ākāśadeśaś ca śabda iti. ekaṃ ca punar ākāśam. ato 'pi na nānādeśeṣu.
api caikarūpye sati deśabhedena kāmaṃ deśā eva bhinnāḥ, na tu śabdaḥ. tasmād ayam apy adoṣaḥ.
children.translated_text:
As for [the objection] that it is impossible for a single existing [entity] to be perceived simultaneously in different places. Consider the sun, dear sir. Though it is one, it appears as if situated in many places. But how is it known that the sun is one? It is replied: <s>Devadatta</s>, facing east, sees the sun before him in the forenoon. One standing to his south does not see two [suns], and [he sees] the present [sun] as being neither oblique nor to the side of <s>Devadatta</s>'s straight line. Therefore, the sun is one. Because of its distance, its location is not determined. Hence the confusion. Similarly with sound too, the location is not determined due to confusion. If the ear were to apprehend the sound by going to the location of the conjunction and disjunction, then at least sometimes its multi-locality would be ascertained. But it does not go to the location of that conjunction. For the ear-cavity is directly perceived as being in its own location. But the aerial conjunctions and disjunctions, being of imperceptible wind, arising at the location of the ear-cavity, are not perceived — so there is nothing impossible. For this very reason there is the confusion that 'sound is in different places.' And sound has space as its locus. And space is one. For this reason too, [sound is] not in different places.
Moreover, when [sounds are] of the same form, even if the locations differ, it is only the locations that are different, not the sound itself. Therefore, this [objection] too is no defect.

children.text: na ca dadhyatrety{*1/338*} atra prakṛtivikārabhāvaḥ. śabdāntaram ikārād yakāraḥ. na hi yakāraṃ prayuñjānā ikāram upādadate, yathā kaṭaṃ cikrīrṣanto vīraṇāni. na ca sādṛśyamātraṃ dṛṣṭvā prakṛtir vikṛtir vocyate. na hi dādhipiṭakaṃ dṛṣṭvā kundapiṭakaṃ ca prakṛtivikārabhāvo 'vagamyate. tasmād ayam apy adoṣaḥ.
children.translated_text: Nor is there a relation of original-and-modified in '<s>dadhyatra</s>.' The '<s>y</s>'-sound is a different phoneme from the '<s>i</s>'-sound. For those who employ the '<s>y</s>'-sound do not take up the '<s>i</s>'-sound — just as those who wish to make a mat [use rushes, not] reeds. Nor can one call something the original and the modification merely from observing similarity. For one does not understand a relation of original-and-modified upon seeing a pot of curds and a pot of jasmine. Therefore, this [objection] too is no defect.

nādavṛddhiparā // MS_1,1.17 //{*1/339*}
yac caitad bahubhir bherīm ādhmanadbhiḥ{*1/340*} śabdam{*1/341*} uccārayadbhir mahāñ śabda upalabhyate, tena pratipuruṣaṃ śabdāvayavapracaya iti gamyate{*1/342*}. naivam. niravayavo hi śabdaḥ avayavabhedānavagamān niravayavatvāc ca mahattvānupapattiḥ. ato na vardhate śabdaḥ. mṛdur ekena [29]{*1/343*} bahubhiś coccāryamāṇe tāny evākṣarāṇi karṇaśaṣkulīmaṇḍalasya sarvāṃ nemiṃ vyāpnuvadbhiḥ saṃyogavibhāgair nairantaryeṇānekaśo grahaṇān mahān ivāvayavavān ivopalabhyante. saṃyogavibhāgā nairantaryeṇa kriyamāṇāḥ śabdam abhivyañjanto nādaśabdavācyāḥ. tena nādasyaiṣā vṛddhiḥ, na śabdasyeti.
children.translated_text: The increase pertains to the resonance (<s>nāda</s>), not to [the sound itself]. // MS 1.1.17 // As for [the objection] that when many persons blow a drum or utter [a sound], a loud sound is perceived, and therefore the accumulation of sound-parts per person is inferred — this is not so. For sound is partless, since no component-distinction is ascertained. And being partless, the impossibility of its becoming loud [follows]. Therefore, sound does not increase. When uttered softly by one and [loudly] by many — those very same phonemes, by conjunctions and disjunctions pervading the entire circumference of the ear-cavity continuously and being apprehended repeatedly — are perceived as if loud, as if having parts. The conjunctions and disjunctions, being continuously produced and manifesting the sound, are called by the term '<s>nāda</s>' (resonance). Therefore, this increase belongs to the <s>nāda</s> (resonance), not to the sound itself.

children.text: nityas tu syād darśanasya parārthatvāt // MS_1,1.18 //
children.translated_text: But [sound] must be eternal, because the manifestation [by utterance] serves another purpose. // MS 1.1.18 //

children.text:
nityaḥ śabdo bhavitum arhati. kutaḥ? darśanasya parārthatvāt. darśanam uccāraṇam, tat parārthaṃ param arthaṃ pratyāyayitum. uccaritamātre hi vinaṣṭe śabde na cānyo 'nyān arthaṃ pratyāyayituṃ śaknuyāt. ato na parārtham uccāryeta. atha na vinaṣṭaḥ, tato bahuśa upalabdhatvād arthāvagama iti yuktam. arthavat sādṛśyād arthāvagama iti cet. na kaścid arthavān, sarveṣāṃ navatvāt. kasyacit pūrvasya kṛtrimaḥ saṃbandho{*1/344*} bhaviṣyatīti cet. tad uktaṃ sadṛśa iti cāvagate vyāmohāt pratyayo vyāvarteta mālāśabdān mālāpratyaya iva{*1/345*}.
yathā gāvīśabdāt sāsnādim iti pratyayasyānivṛttiḥ, tadvad bhaviṣyatīti cet. na hi gośabdaṃ tatroccārayitum icchā. nehānyaśabdoccicārayiṣā. na caikenoccāraṇāyatnena{*1/346*} saṃvyavahāraś cārthasaṃbandhaś ca śakyate{*1/347*} kartum. tasmād darśanasya parārthatvāt, nityaḥ śabdaḥ.
children.translated_text:
Sound ought to be eternal. Why? Because the manifestation serves another purpose (<s>parārtha</s>). 'Manifestation' here means utterance; that serves another purpose — namely, to communicate a meaning. For if the sound perished the very instant it was uttered, one person could not communicate a meaning to another. Therefore, it would not be uttered for another's sake. But if it has not perished, then — since it has been perceived many times — the understanding of meaning is justified.
[Objection:] The understanding of meaning arises from similarity with a meaningful [sound previously heard]. [Reply:] No [previous sound] is meaningful, since all are new [productions]. [Objection:] The artificial relation of some prior [sound] will [serve as the basis]. [Reply:] That was [already] addressed: 'if a similar [but different entity] is apprehended, the cognition would be reversed through confusion — just as from the word "<s>mālā</s>" (garland), a cognition of garlands [might arise from the word] "<s>śālā</s>" (hall).'
[Objection:] Just as from the word '<s>go</s>' (cow), the cognition of an animal with a dewlap, etc. is not reversed, so too it will be [stable]. [Reply:] No, for one does not wish to utter the word '<s>go</s>' there [in a new sense]; nor here does one wish to utter another word. Nor is it possible, with a single effort of utterance, to both establish conventional usage and communicate a meaning. Therefore, because manifestation serves another purpose, sound is eternal.

children.translated_text: Because of simultaneity everywhere. // MS 1.1.19 //

children.text: gośabda uccarite sarvagavīṣu yugapat pratyayo bhavati. ata ākṛtivacano 'yam. na cākṛtyā śabdasya saṃbandhaḥ śakyate kartum. nirdiśya hy ākṛtiṃ kartā saṃbadhnīyāt. gopiṇḍe ca bahūnām ākṛtīnāṃ sadbhāvāc chabdam antareṇa gośabdavācyāṃ vibhaktām ākṛtiṃ kena prakāreṇopadekṣyati? nitye tu sati gośabde bahukṛtva [30]{*1/348*} uccaritaḥ śrutapūrvaś cānyāsu govyaktiṣv anvayavyatirekābhyām ākṛtivacanam avagamiṣyati. tasmād api nityaḥ.
children.translated_text: When the word 'go' (cow) is uttered, a cognition arises simultaneously in regard to all cows. Therefore this [word] denotes the universal form (<s>ākṛti</s>). But the relation of a word with a universal form cannot be created [artificially]. For one who would create the relation would have to point out the universal form [separately]. And since in the aggregate of 'cow' (<s>go-piṇḍa</s>) many universal forms exist, by what means would one, without [already having] the word, point out the particular universal form that is to be denoted by the word 'go'? But if the word 'go' is eternal, then having been uttered many times and having been heard before, one will understand by the method of agreement and difference (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>) that it denotes the universal form in other individual cows. Therefore, from this too, [the word] is eternal.

children.text:
aṣṭakṛtvo gośabda uccarita iti vadanti, nāṣṭau gośabdā iti. kim ato, yady evam. anena vacanenāvagamyate, pratyabhijānantīti{*1/349*}. vayaṃ tāvat pratyabhijānīmo na naḥ karaṇadaurbalyam. evam anye 'pi pratyabhijānanti. sa evāyam iti. pratyabhijānānā{*1/350*} vayam ivānye 'pi nānya iti vaktum arhanti.
atha matam anyatve sati sādṛśyena vyāmūḍhāḥ sa iti vakṣyanti. tan na. na hi te sadṛśa iti pratiyanti, kiṃ tarhi sa evāyam iti. vidite ca sphuṭe 'nyatve vyāmoha iti gamyate. na cāyam anya iti praty-akṣam anyad vā pramāṇam asti.
syād etat - buddhikarmaṇī api te pratyabhijñāyete. te 'pi nitye prāpnutaḥ. naiṣa doṣaḥ. na hi te pratyakṣe. atha pratyakṣe nitye eva{*1/351*}. hy astanasya śabdasya vināśād anyo 'dyatana iti cet. naiṣa vinaṣṭaḥ, yata enaṃ punar upalabhāmahe. na hi pratyakṣadṛṣṭaṃ muhūrtam adṛṣṭvā punar upalabhyamānaṃ pratyabhijānanto vinaṣṭaṃ parikalpayanti. parikalpayanto dvitīyasaṃdarśane mātari, jāyāyāṃ pitari vā nāśvasyuḥ. na hy anupalambhamātreṇa nāstīty avagamya naṣṭa ity eva kalpayanti. apramāṇatāyāṃ viditāyāṃ nāstīty avagacchāmaḥ. na hi pramāṇe pratyakṣe saty apramāṇatā syāt. astīti punar avyāmohenāvagamyamāne na kvacid apy abhāvaḥ. na cāsiddhe 'bhāve vyāmohaḥ, na ca siddho 'bhāvaḥ. tasmād asati vyāmohe, nābhāvaḥ{*1/352*}. tad e[31]{*1/353*}tad ānupūrvyā siddham. tasmāt purastād anuccāritam anupalabhamānā api na vinaṣṭa ity avagantum arhanti. yathā{*1/354*} gṛhān nirgatāḥ sarvagṛhajanam apaśyantaḥ punaḥ praviśyopalabhamānā api na prāk praveśād vinaṣṭa ity avagacchanti. tadvad enam api nānya iti vaktum arhanti. ye 'pi sarveṣāṃ bhāvānāṃ pratikṣaṇaṃ vināśam abhyupagacchanti, te 'pi na śaknuvanti śabdasya vaditum. ante hi kṣayadarśanāt te manyante. na ca śabdasyānto na ca kṣayo lakṣyate. sa iti pratyakṣaḥ pratyayaḥ sadṛśa ity ānumānikaḥ. na ca pratyakṣaviruddham anumānam udeti. svakāryaṃ vā sādhayati. tasmān nityaḥ.
children.translated_text:
They say 'the word "go" has been uttered eight times,' not 'eight "go"-words [have been uttered].' What follows from this? By this expression one understands that 'they recognize [it as the same].' We, for our part, recognize it [as the same] — there is no weakness in our cognitive faculties. Others too recognize it in the same way — 'this is that very same one.' Those who recognize it [as the same], like us, cannot justifiably say 'it is another.'
If one thinks: 'Being [actually] different, they will say "the same" because they are confused by similarity' — that is not so. For they do not cognize [it as] 'similar,' but rather as 'this is that very same one.' And confusion is understood [only] when the difference is known and manifest. But there is no direct perception or other valid means of knowledge [to establish] that 'this is another.'
It may be objected: Cognition and action (<s>buddhi-karmaṇī</s>) too are recognized [as the same across instances]; they too would turn out to be eternal. This is no fault. For they are not directly perceived [as continuing]. But if they are directly perceived — then they are indeed eternal. [If one objects:] 'Yesterday's word has perished, and today's is another' — this [word] has not perished, since we perceive it again. For those who recognize something directly perceived, and [which] after not being seen for a moment is perceived again, do not imagine it to have perished. Were they to imagine so, they would not rest assured at the second sighting of a mother, wife, or father. For they do not, merely from non-perception alone, judge 'it does not exist' and then imagine 'it has perished.' When the lack of valid evidence [for non-existence] is known, we understand 'it does not not-exist.' For where there is direct perception as valid evidence [for existence], there cannot be an absence of valid evidence. And when 'it exists' is understood without confusion, there is no absence anywhere. And without an established absence, there is no confusion; nor is absence established. Therefore, in the absence of confusion, there is no non-existence. This has been established step by step. Therefore, even those who, prior to [the word's] utterance, do not perceive it [and thus do] not apprehend it, ought not to conclude that it has perished. Just as those who have gone outside the house, not seeing any household member, upon re-entering and perceiving them, do not conclude that they had perished before re-entry — similarly, they cannot justifiably say that this [word] is another. Even those who accept the momentary destruction of all entities cannot say [this] of the word. For they hold [momentariness] because of seeing destruction at the end [of an entity's existence]. But neither an end nor a destruction of the word is observed. The cognition 'it is the same' is direct perception; [the cognition] 'it is similar' is inferential. And an inference contradicting direct perception does not arise, nor does it accomplish its own purpose. Therefore, [the word] is eternal.

children.text: anapekṣatvāt // MS_1,1.21 //
children.translated_text: Because [the word] does not depend [on any cause for its destruction]. // MS_1,1.21 //

children.text: yeṣām anavagatotpattīnāṃ dravyāṇāṃ bhāva eva lakṣyate, teṣām api keṣāṃcid anityatā gamyate, yeṣāṃ vināśakāraṇam upalabhyate. yathābhinavaṃ paṭaṃ dṛṣṭvā, na caivaṃ kriyamāṇam upalabdhavān, athavānityatvam avagacchati rūpam eva dṛṣṭvā, tantuvyatiṣaṅgajanito 'yaṃ tantuvyatiṣaṅgavināśāt tantuvināśād vā vinaśyatīty avagacchati. naivaṃ śabdasya kiṃcit kāraṇam avagamyate, yad vināśād vinaṅkṣyatīty avagamyate.
children.translated_text: Even in the case of substances whose origination is not known but whose existence alone is observed, the impermanence of some is understood — namely, those for which a cause of destruction is perceived. For example, upon seeing a new cloth, even without having observed it being made, one still understands its impermanence from seeing its form alone — one understands that 'this, produced from the interweaving of threads, will perish from the destruction of the interweaving or from the destruction of the threads.' But for the word, no such cause is perceived, from whose destruction [one could infer that] the word would perish.

children.text: prakhyābhāvāc ca yogasya // MS_1,1.22 //
children.translated_text: And because of the non-manifestation of a connection [with any material cause]. // MS_1,1.22 //

children.text: idaṃ padebhyaḥ kebhyaścid uttaraṃ sūtram. nanu vāyukāraṇakaḥ syād iti vāyur udgataḥ saṃyogavibhāgaiḥ śabdo bhavatīti. tathā ca śikṣākārā āhuḥ - vāyur āpadyate śabdatām iti{*1/355*}. naitad evam. vāyavīyaś cec chabdo bhaved, vāyoḥ saṃniveśaviśeṣaḥ syāt. na ca vāyavīyān avayavāñ śabde sataḥ pratyabhijānīmo yathā paṭasya tantumayān. na caivaṃ bhavati. syāc ced evam, sparśa-ne[32]{*1/356*}nopalabhemahi. na ca vāyavīyān avayavāñ śabdagatān spṛśāmaḥ. tasmān na vāyukāraṇakaḥ. ato nityaḥ.
children.translated_text: This <s>sūtra</s> is a sequel to certain preceding ones. [Objection:] Perhaps [the word] has air (<s>vāyu</s>) as its [material] cause — [the theory being that] air, having risen up, produces sound through conjunction and disjunction. And thus the <s>śikṣā</s>-authors (phoneticians) say: 'Air transforms into sound.' This is not so. If sound were an air-product, it would be a particular configuration of air. But we do not recognize in the existing sound any air-components, as we [recognize] thread-components in cloth. Nor does it happen thus. Were it so, we would perceive [the air-components] by touch. But we do not touch any air-components residing in sound. Therefore, [sound] does not have air as its material cause. Hence, [it is] eternal.

children.translated_text: And because of the observation of an indicatory sign (<s>liṅga</s>). // MS_1,1.23 //

children.text: liṅgaṃ caiva bhavati, vācā virūpanityayeti{*1/357*}. anyaparaṃ hīdaṃ vākyaṃ vāco nityatām anuvadati. tasmān nityaḥ śabdaḥ.

children.text:
yady apy autpattiko nityaḥ śabdo arthasaṃbandhaś ca{*1/359*}, tathāpi na codanālakṣaṇo dharmaḥ. codanā hi vākyam. na hy agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāma ity ato vākyād anyatamāt{*1/360*} padād agnihotrāt svargo bhavatīti gamyate. gamyate tu padatraya uccarite. na cātra caturthaḥ śabdo 'sty anyad ataḥ padatrayasamudāyāt. na cāyaṃ samudāyo 'sti loke, yato 'sya vyavahārād artho 'vagamyate. padāny amūni prayuktāni, teṣāṃ nityo 'rthaḥ. aprayuktaś ca samudāyaḥ. tasmāt samudāyasyārthaḥ kṛtrimo vyāmoho vā. na ca padārthā eva vākyārthaḥ. sāmānye hi padaṃ pravartate, viśeṣe vākyam. anyac ca sāmānyam, anyo viśeṣaḥ. na ca padārthād vākyārthāvagatiḥ, asaṃbandhāt. asati cet saṃbandhe kasmiṃścit padārthe 'vagate 'rthāntaram avagamyeta, ekasminn avagate sarvam avagataṃ syāt. na caitad evaṃ bhavati. tasmād anyo vākyārthaḥ.
syād etat - aprayuktād api vākyād asati saṃbandhe svabhāvād arthāvagama iti. yadi kalpyeta - śabdo dharmam ātmīyaṃ vyutkrāmet. na caiṣa śabdadharmo yad aprayuktād api śabdārthaḥ pratīyate. na hi [33]{*1/361*} prathamaśrutāt kutaścic chabdāt kecid arthaṃ pratiyanti. tad abhidhīyate - padadharmo 'yaṃ na vākyadharmaḥ. vākyād dhi prathamāvagatād api pratiyanto 'rthaṃ dṛśyante. naitad evam. yadi prathamaśrutād avagaccheyuḥ, api tarhi sarve 'vagaccheyuḥ padārthavido 'nye ca. na tv apadārthavido 'vagacchanti. tasmān naitad evam. nanu padārthavadbhir apy avagacchadbhir akṛta eva vākyārthasaṃbandho bhaviṣyati. padārthavedanena hi saṃskṛtā avagamiśyanti, yathā tam eva padārthaṃ dvitīyādiśravaṇeneti. neti brūmaḥ. yadi vākye 'ntyo varṇaḥ pūrvavarṇajanitasaṃskārasahitaḥ padārthebhyo 'rthāntaraṃ pratyāyayati, upakāras tu tadānīṃ{*1/362*} padārthajñānād avakalpate. tasmāt kṛtrimo vākyārthapratyayo vyāmoho vā. na padārthadvāreṇa saṃbhavati vākyārthajñānam iti. nanv evaṃ bhaviṣyati sāmānyavācinaḥ padasya gaur{*1/363*} iti vāśva iti vā, viśeṣakaṃ śukla iti vā kṛṣṇa iti vā padam antikād upanipatati yadā, tadā vākyārtho 'vagamyate. tan na. na hi{*1/364*} katham iva gaur iti vāśva iti vā sāmānyavācinaḥ padāt sarvagavīṣu sarvāśveṣu ca buddhir upasarpantī śrutijanitā, vākyānurodhena kutaścid viśeṣād apavarteta. na ca śukla ityāder viśeṣavacanasya kṛṣṇādi-nivṛttir bhavati śabdārthaḥ. na cānarthako mā bhūd ity arthaparikalpanā śakyā. ato na padārthajanito vākyārthaḥ. tasmāt kṛtrimaḥ. padasaṃghātāḥ khalv ete saṃghātāś ca puruṣakṛtā dṛśyante, yathā -
children.translated_text:
Even though the word and its relation to meaning are innate (<s>autpattika</s>) and eternal, still <s>Dharma</s> is not characterized by injunction (<s>codanā</s>). For an injunction is a sentence. For from the sentence 'One who desires heaven should offer the <s>Agnihotra</s>,' it is not understood from any single word — from 'Agnihotra' [alone] — that 'from the <s>Agnihotra</s> arises heaven.' It is understood [only] when the three words are uttered [together]. And here there is no fourth word beyond the aggregate of these three words. And this aggregate does not exist in common usage, from whose conventional use the meaning could be understood. These individual words have been used [before], and their meaning is eternal. But the aggregate has not been used [before]. Therefore, the meaning of the aggregate is either artificial or a delusion. And the meaning of the individual words is not [identical with] the sentence-meaning. For a word operates in the domain of the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), a sentence in the domain of the particular (<s>viśeṣa</s>). And the universal is one thing, the particular another. And there is no comprehension of sentence-meaning from word-meaning, because of the absence of a [direct] connection. If, in the absence of connection, upon understanding one word-meaning another meaning were comprehended, then upon understanding one [meaning], all would be comprehended. But this does not happen. Therefore, sentence-meaning is something different.
It may be objected: Even from a previously unused sentence, in the absence of a [prior] connection, meaning is understood by its own nature. If [this were] postulated — the word would transgress its own nature. And it is not the nature of a word that meaning is understood even from a word that has not been [previously] used. For nobody understands any meaning from some word heard for the first time. To this it is said: This is a property of words, not of sentences. For people are seen to understand meaning even from a sentence heard for the first time. This is not so. If they understood from a sentence heard for the first time, then all — those who know word-meanings and those who do not — would understand. But those who do not know word-meanings do not understand. Therefore this is not so. [Objection:] Even for those who know word-meanings and do understand, the sentence-meaning connection may well be uncreated [i.e., innate]. For those refined by knowledge of word-meanings will understand, just as [they understand] that very same word-meaning upon hearing it a second time and so on. We reply: No. If in a sentence the final phoneme, together with the impressions generated by prior phonemes, causes understanding of a meaning different from the word-meanings — then the contribution of word-meaning knowledge is established at that point. Therefore, the cognition of sentence-meaning is either artificial or a delusion. Sentence-meaning knowledge does not arise through the medium of word-meaning. [Objection:] It will be thus: When a generic word like 'go' (cow) or 'aśva' (horse) is joined by a qualifying word like 'śukla' (white) or 'kṛṣṇa' (black), then sentence-meaning is understood. [Reply:] No. For how could the cognition generated by hearing the generic word 'go' or 'aśva,' which extends to all cows or all horses, be redirected from some particular [subset] in accordance with the sentence? Nor is the exclusion of black and the like the word-meaning of the qualifier 'white.' Nor can meaning be fabricated [merely] so that [the word] is not meaningless. Therefore, sentence-meaning is not generated from word-meanings. Hence it is artificial. These word-combinations are indeed combinations, and combinations are seen to be man-made, as for example —

children.translated_text:
The pronouncing together of existing, present words for the purpose of action with reference to those very same objects. A sentence is not understood as conveying a different meaning independently of and apart from the word-meanings. Why? Because of the absence of a means of valid knowledge. There is no means of valid knowledge by which we could establish [such an independent sentence-meaning]. For the final phoneme of a sentence, when it does not take into account the word-meanings and is devoid of the impressions generated by the preceding phonemes, has no capacity to convey anything other than the word-meanings.
[Objection:] But there is postulation (<s>arthāpatti</s>) — we understand a meaning distinct from the word-meanings, and without the capacity [of the sentence as a whole], that cannot be explained. [Reply:] No. Because the meaning has that [viz., the word-meanings] as its basis. Postulation would be valid if, even in the absence of such capacity, no other cause could be posited. But a cause is perceived. What? The word-meanings. For words, having expressed their respective word-meanings, have completed their function. Then the word-meanings, being understood, convey the sentence-meaning. How? When a quality such as 'white' or 'black' is perceived, it is indeed sufficient to produce a cognition of the quality-possessor. Therefore, those who wish to produce a cognition of the quality-possessor utter merely the quality-word. Their intention, as conceived, will be fulfilled — there will be a cognition of the qualified meaning. And the cognition of the qualified meaning is the sentence-meaning. If it is understood thus that the sentence-meaning [arises] from another [source], who would ever say that an unseen capacity of the word-aggregate is inferred from the meaning?
Moreover, this is understood through co-presence and co-absence (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>). For sometimes this condition occurs — even from a mental [cause], a depositor [of impressions] — that the word-meanings are not ascertained from the uttered words. Then they would necessarily not understand the sentence-meaning — if [the sentence] had no dependence on the separate [word-meanings]. But they necessarily do not understand. Furthermore, even without the utterance of words, one who understands whiteness understands the thing possessing the white quality. Therefore, the sentence-meaning is just the cognition of word-meanings. It has no relation with the word-aggregate.
As for [the objection] that 'the verbally conveyed word-meaning should not be deflected from any specific [meaning] by dependence on the sentence' — true, this is so. But where the word-meaning alone, being employed in isolation, would be purposeless due to the absence of any purpose — there, the qualification is understood to the extent that 'let there be a sentence-meaning too' — not everywhere. And this being so, the objection that 'the exclusion of other qualities is not a word-meaning' is also answered.
Moreover, the second case-ending (<s>dvitīyā</s>) and the like, which occur after the nominal stem, are qualifiers of the nominal-stem-meaning — so he says. And that specific meaning [conveyed by the case-ending] would override the general meaning [conveyed by the stem alone]. As for [the objection] that 'these word-aggregates are seen to be man-made' — that has been answered by [arguments involving] non-remembrance and the like. Moreover, human beings have no seed [i.e., no original source] for constructing sentences of this kind [regarding <s>Dharma</s>].

children.translated_text:
It was stated: '<s>Dharma</s> is that purpose characterized by Vedic injunction (<s>codanā</s>)' — because the relation of word to meaning is not man-made. The objection based on words and sentences has been answered. Now we shall raise another type of objection. We say: the injunctions are man-made (<s>pauruṣeya</s>), the <s>Vedas</s> are of recent origin, fabricated, and now in their present extent; and they are aggregates of injunctions. If the <s>Vedas</s> are man-made, then the injunctions are undoubtedly man-made.
But how do some think the <s>Vedas</s> are fabricated? Because they are designated by persons — for the <s>Vedas</s> are named after persons: '<s>Kāṭhaka</s>' [from <s>Kaṭha</s>], '<s>Kālāpaka</s>' [from <s>Kalāpa</s>], '<s>Paippalādaka</s>' [from <s>Pippalāda</s>], '<s>Mauhula</s>' [from <s>Muhula</s>]. And there is no naming without a relation, and there is no relation between a person and a word other than the maker being the person and the product being the word. [Objection:] Perhaps the naming might be based on teaching [rather than authorship]. [Reply:] We say no. For the distinguishing mark must be exclusive — one alone is the author, but many might teach. Therefore, even if the author of the injunction is not remembered, [the <s>Vedas</s>] would have an author. Therefore, the object characterized by injunction is not a valid means of knowledge for <s>Dharma</s>.

children.text: yad uktam - kartṛlakṣaṇā samākhyā kāṭhakādyeti. tad ucyate - neyam arthāpattiḥ, akartṛbhir api hy enām ācakṣīran, prakarṣeṇa vacanam (ananyasādhāraṇaṃ){*1/392*} kaṭhādibhir anuṣṭhitaṃ syāt, tathāpi hi samākhyātāro bhavanti. smaryate ca vaiśaṃpāyanaḥ sarvaśākhādhyāyī, kaṭhaḥ punar imāṃ kevalāṃ śākhām adhyāpayāṃ babhūveti. sa bahuśākhādhyāyināṃ saṃnidhāv ekaśākhādhyāyy anyāṃ śākhām anadhīyānaḥ, tasyāṃ prakṛṣṭatvād asādhāraṇam upapadyate viśeṣaṇam.
children.translated_text: As for what was said — that the designation such as '<s>Kāṭhaka</s>' and the like is indicative of an author — to that it is replied: This is not a case of postulation (<s>arthāpatti</s>). For even non-authors could designate them [thus]. The 'distinguished teaching' — the preeminent recitation, exclusive to <s>Kaṭha</s> and the like — may have been carried out [by them]; and thus they become [the text's] designators. And it is traditionally remembered that <s>Vaiśaṃpāyana</s> studied all the branches, while <s>Kaṭha</s> taught only this one particular branch. He, being a student of a single branch in the presence of those who studied many branches, not studying any other branch — his exclusive designation with respect to that [branch] is justified because of his preeminence therein.

(na tv asya samudāyaḥ kvacit siddhaḥ.){*1/393*} ikāras tu yathaivāpatye siddhas tathā kriyāyām api kartari. tasmād yaḥ pravāhayati, sa prāvāhaṇiḥ. babara iti śabdānukṛtiḥ. tena yo nityārthas tam evaitau śabdau vadiṣyataḥ. ata uktam - paraṃ tu śrutisāmānyamātram iti.
children.translated_text: As for [the argument based on] '<s>Prāvāhaṇi</s>' — no, because the person <s>Pravāhaṇa</s> is not established [as existing]. [The word] '<s>Prāvāhaṇi</s>' is not the offspring of <s>Pravāhaṇa</s>. The prefix 'pra-' is established in the sense of eminence, and the root 'vah-' in the sense of carrying. (Nor is the combination of these [as a personal name] established anywhere.) And the suffix '-i' is established in the sense of an agent of action, just as it is in the sense of offspring. Therefore, <s>Prāvāhaṇi</s> means 'one who carries forth eminently.' '<s>Babara</s>' is an onomatopoeic word. Therefore, these words will denote only an eternal meaning. Hence it is stated: 'But the other [argument proves] merely a similarity of sound.'

atha katham avagamyate nāyam unmattabālavākyasadṛśa iti. tathā [38]{*1/394*} hi paśyāmaḥ - vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata, sarpāḥ satram āsata iti. yathā - jarad gavo gāyati mattakāni, kathaṃ nāma jarad gavo gāyeta. kathaṃ vā vanaspatayaḥ sarpā vā satram āsīrann iti. ucyate - viniyuktaṃ hi dṛśyate, paraspareṇa saṃbandhārtham. katham. jyotiṣṭoma ity abhidhāya kartavya ity ucyate. kenety ākāṅkṣite someneti. kim artham iti, svargāyeti. katham iti. ittham, (anayeti kartavyatayā){*1/395*} iti. evam avagacchantaḥ, padārthair ebhiḥ saṃskṛtaṃ piṇḍitaṃ vākyārthaṃ katham unmattabālavākyasadṛśam iti vakṣyāmaḥ.
nanv anupapannam idaṃ dṛśyate - vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata ityevamādi. nānupapannam. na, anena agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāma ity evamādayo 'nupapannāḥ syuḥ. api ca vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata ityevamādayo 'pi nānupapannāḥ, stutayo hy etāḥ satrasya, vanaspatayo nāmācetanā idaṃ satram upāsitavantaḥ, kiṃ punar vṛddhāṃso brāhmaṇāḥ. tad yathā loke - sandhyāyāṃ mṛgā api na caranti, kiṃ punar vidvāṃso brāhmaṇā iti. api cāvigītaḥ suhṛdupadeśaḥ supratiṣṭhitaḥ katham ivāśaṅketonmattabālavākyasadṛśa iti. tasmāc codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharma iti siddham.
children.translated_text:
But how is it understood that this [Vedic text] is not like the speech of the mad or of children? For thus we observe: 'The trees sat in a sacrificial session,' 'The serpents sat in a sacrificial session.' Or: '<s>Jarad-gava</s> sings the <s>mattakāni</s>' — how indeed would <s>Jarad-gava</s> sing? And how would trees or serpents sit in a sacrificial session?
It is replied: For [the text] is seen to be applied — each part having a connection with the others for the purpose of mutual relation. How? Having stated '<s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s>,' it is said 'is to be performed.' By whom? — when one inquires, [the answer is:] 'with <s>Soma</s>.' For what purpose? 'For heaven.' How? 'In this manner, by this procedure.' Understanding thus, how shall we say that the sentence-meaning, which is refined and synthesized from these word-meanings, is like the speech of the mad or of children?
[Objection:] But what is observed [in the <s>Veda</s>] is untenable — 'the trees sat in a sacrificial session' and the like. [Reply:] It is not untenable. No — [for if it were], then 'let the one desiring heaven perform the <s>Agnihotra</s>' and similar passages would also be untenable. Moreover, 'the trees sat in a sacrificial session' and similar passages are not untenable either, for they are laudatory passages (<s>stuti</s>) of the sacrificial session: 'Those called "trees," which are insentient, performed this session — how much more then the mature <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>!' Just as in common parlance: 'At twilight even the animals do not move about — how much more then the learned <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>!' Moreover, a well-tested friend's advice, well-established [in reliability] — how could it be suspected of being like the speech of the mad or of children? Therefore, '<s>Dharma</s> is the purpose characterized by Vedic injunction' — this is established.

children.text: āmnāyasya kriyārthatvād ānarthakyam atadarthānāṃ tasmād anityam ucyate // MS_1,2.1 //
children.translated_text: Since the revealed scripture (<s>Āmnāya</s>) has action as its purpose, those [passages] which do not serve that purpose are useless; therefore, [such passages] are said to be non-eternal [i.e., subsidiary]. // MS 1.2.1 //

children.text: so 'rodīd yad arodīt, tad rudrasya rudratvam{*1/397*}; prajāpatir ātmano vapām udakhidat{*1/398*}. devā vai devayajanam adhyavasāya diśo na prājānan{*1/399*} ityevamādīni samāmnātāraḥ samāmananti vākyāni. tāni kiṃ kaṃcid dharmaṃ pramimate uta neti bhavati vicāraṇā. tad abhidhīyate - kriyā katham anuṣṭheyeti tāṃ vadituṃ{*1/400*} samāmnātāro vākyāni samāmananti. tad yāni vākyāni kriyāṃ nāvagamayanti kriyāsaṃbaddhaṃ vā kiṃcit, evam eva bhūtam artham anvācakṣate - ruditavān rudraḥ; vapām uccikheda prajāpatiḥ; devā vai diśo na prajajñira ityevaṃjātīyakāni, tāni kaṃ dharmaṃ pramimīran. athocyeta - adhyāhāreṇa vā vipariṇāmena vā vyavahitakalpanayā vā vyavadhāraṇakalpanayā vā guṇakalpanayā vā kaścid arthaḥ kalpāyiṣyata iti. sa kalpyamānaḥ kaḥ kalpyeta - rudraḥ kila ruroda, ato 'nyenāpi roditavyam. uccikhedātmavapāṃ{*1/401*} prajāpatiḥ, ato 'nyo 'py utkhided ātmano vapām. devā vai devayajanakāle diśo na prajñātavantaḥ, ato 'nyo 'pi diśo na prajānīyād iti, tac cāśakyam, iṣṭaviyogenābhighātena vā yad bāṣpanirmocanam, tad rodanam ity ucyate, na ca, tad icchāto bhavati. na ca kaści[40]{*1/402*}d ātmano vapām utkhidya tām agnau prahṛtya tata utthitena tūpareṇa paśuṇā yaṣṭuṃ śaknuyāt. na ca{*1/403*}, devayajanādhyavasānakāle kecid diśo muhyeyuḥ. ata eṣām ānarthakyam. tasmād evaṃjātīyakāni vākyāny anityānīty ucyante, (yady api ca nityāni, tathāpi na nityam arthaṃ kurvanti){*1/404*} iti. sa eṣa vākyaikadeśasyākṣepaḥ, na kṛtsnasya vākyasya. nanv ekadeśād vinā sākāṅkṣaḥ padasamūho na paryāptaḥ svasmai prayojanāya, ata ākṣipta eveti. naivam, bhavati hi kaścit padasamūhaḥ, yo 'rthavādebhyo vināpi vidadhāti kaṃcid artham, yāni punas taiḥ saha saṃyujyārthāntare vartante, tāny ekadeśākṣepeṇākṣipyate.
children.translated_text: He wept — because he wept, that is the <s>Rudra</s>-hood of <s>Rudra</s>; <s>Prajāpati</s> tore out the fat from his own body. The gods, having resolved upon the place of sacrifice, did not know the directions — such and similar sentences are traditionally recited by the traditionists. The question arises: do these establish any <s>Dharma</s> or not? That is now addressed — the traditionists recite sentences in order to state how a ritual action is to be performed. Now, those sentences that do not convey any ritual action or anything connected with ritual action, but merely narrate a fact as it occurred — '<s>Rudra</s> wept; <s>Prajāpati</s> tore out the fat; the gods did not know the directions' — of this kind, what <s>Dharma</s> could they establish? If it were said that some meaning could be constructed through ellipsis, transformation, postulation of an intervening [element], postulation of a restriction, or postulation of a subordinate [meaning] — then what could be so constructed? [Could one say:] '<s>Rudra</s> indeed wept, therefore others too should weep; <s>Prajāpati</s> tore out his own fat, therefore another too should tear out his own fat; the gods did not know the directions at the time of the sacrifice, therefore another too should not know the directions' — but this is impossible. For weeping is the shedding of tears caused by separation from a desired [object] or by affliction, and it does not occur by will. Nor could anyone, having torn out the fat from his own body and offered it into the fire, sacrifice with the animal that would arise from the rising vapor. Nor would anyone become confused about directions at the time of resolving upon the place of sacrifice. Therefore these [sentences] are purposeless. Hence sentences of this kind are called non-eternal (i.e., not permanently valid), (and even if they are eternal, they do not produce an eternal purpose). This is a rejection of a part of the sentence, not of the entire sentence. [Objection:] But without a part, the remaining collection of words is syntactically incomplete and insufficient for its own purpose; hence it too is rejected. [Reply:] Not so, for there is indeed a collection of words that prescribes some meaning even without the <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory) portions; but those [sentences] that, being joined with them, function in a different meaning — those are rejected through the rejection of a part.
